entries.title: HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110)
entries.why: The standard itself, so it settles arguments about idempotency, safe methods, and what 301 versus 302 actually mean rather than what blog posts claim they mean.

entries.title: The WebSocket Protocol (RFC 6455)
entries.why: Defines the handshake and framing precisely, which is the boundary between what the protocol gives you and what your chat architecture still has to solve itself.

entries.title: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)
entries.why: The normative source for handshake properties and round-trip counts, which matters whenever you are estimating connection setup latency.

entries.title: Domain Names: Concepts and Facilities (RFC 1034)
entries.why: Defines delegation, caching, and TTL semantics, including the negative-caching behaviour that surprises people bringing up a new subdomain.

entries.title: Universally Unique Identifiers (RFC 9562)
entries.why: The current UUID standard, and the definitive statement of what UUIDv7 guarantees about time ordering, which is the usual alternative to Snowflake.

entries.title: Robots Exclusion Protocol (RFC 9309)
entries.why: Standardises robots.txt parsing, and makes explicit that it is a politeness protocol rather than an access-control mechanism.

entries.title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749)
entries.why: The source for what OAuth actually specifies, which is authorization rather than authentication — a distinction candidates routinely get backwards.

entries.title: JSON Web Token (RFC 7519)
entries.why: Defines what a JWT is and is not, which matters for the common claim that stateless tokens make session revocation free.

entries.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
entries.why: The primary source for consistent hashing with virtual nodes, sloppy quorums, vector clocks, and anti-entropy — most secondhand explanations of these blur the details.

entries.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)
entries.why: The clearest primary treatment of leader election and replicated logs, and the reference point for why fencing prevents split brain.

entries.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
entries.why: The original description of the model, including combiners and speculative execution for stragglers, both of which are usually omitted from summaries.

entries.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
entries.why: The origin of the wide-column model that message storage designs borrow, including why partition and clustering keys determine your read pattern.

entries.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
entries.why: The counterexample to the folklore that distributed systems cannot offer strong consistency, and an honest account of what it costs to get it.

entries.title: TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph
entries.why: A production account of serving a social graph at scale, and why the read path is optimised so aggressively relative to writes.

entries.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook
entries.why: The best real-world treatment of cache stampedes, leases, and the failure modes that only appear once a cache tier is genuinely large.

entries.title: How to do distributed locking
entries.why: The standard critique of using Redis locks for correctness, and the source of the fencing-token argument. Essential counterweight to the Redis lock documentation.

entries.title: Please stop calling databases CP or AP
entries.why: Explains why the casual CP/AP labelling most interview material uses is not meaningful, which is the single most common inaccuracy in this subject.

entries.title: Jepsen Analyses
entries.why: Empirical testing of what databases actually guarantee under partition, as opposed to what their marketing claims. The reference for checking a consistency claim.

entries.title: PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation
entries.why: Precise definitions of each isolation level and the anomalies each one still permits, including why Read Committed does not stop lost updates.

entries.title: PostgreSQL: Indexes
entries.why: Covers multicolumn index ordering and when the planner can use an index at all, which is the mechanism behind most 'why is this query slow' answers.

entries.title: Apache Kafka Documentation
entries.why: Authoritative on partitions, consumer groups, and delivery semantics, including the limits of what Kafka's exactly-once actually covers.

entries.title: Redis Documentation
entries.why: Reference for atomic operations, Lua scripting, and expiration — the primitives that make a correct rate limiter possible on a single round trip.

entries.title: Apache Cassandra Documentation
entries.why: A production implementation of the Dynamo ideas, useful for checking how quorum tuning and partition keys behave in practice rather than in theory.

entries.title: Amazon S3: Multipart Upload Overview
entries.why: Defines part sizes, limits, and retry behaviour, which is the concrete detail behind 'chunk the upload so a failure does not restart it'.

entries.title: Amazon S3: Using Presigned URLs
entries.why: The mechanism that lets clients upload directly to storage without the API proxying bytes, plus the expiry semantics that bound the risk.

entries.title: Cloudflare Cache Documentation
entries.why: Concrete edge behaviour for cache keys, TTLs, and purging — particularly the cache-key rules behind query-string collisions.

entries.title: HTTP Live Streaming
entries.why: The reference for manifests, segments, and adaptive bitrate, which is why transcoding fans out into multiple renditions at all.

entries.title: Firebase Cloud Messaging
entries.why: Authoritative on device tokens, provider feedback, and the delivery guarantees a push channel actually offers, which are weaker than most designs assume.

entries.title: gRPC Core Concepts
entries.why: Defines streaming modes, deadlines, and status codes, which is the substance behind choosing RPC over REST for internal calls.

entries.title: Kubernetes: Service
entries.why: How service discovery and virtual IPs actually work in the most common orchestrator, rather than as an abstract registry concept.

entries.title: Envoy: Load Balancing Architecture
entries.why: A precise description of real load-balancing policies including outlier detection, which is what health checking looks like in production.

entries.title: OpenTelemetry Documentation
entries.why: The vocabulary for metrics, logs, and traces, and why tail latency needs tracing rather than averages to diagnose.

entries.title: OWASP Top Ten
entries.why: The common reference for the risks a design review is expected to name, and specific enough to check a design against rather than gesture at.

entries.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard
entries.why: Turns 'we should be secure' into enumerated verifiable controls, which is the difference between a checklist and an actual security argument.

entries.title: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives
entries.why: Defines SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets properly, including why an availability target is a product decision rather than an engineering one.

entries.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures
entries.why: The definitive treatment of how retries and overload interact to take a system down, and why load shedding beats queueing under saturation.

entries.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
entries.why: The clearest primary explanation of why jitter is not optional, with the reasoning for how retry storms synchronise without it.

entries.title: The Amazon Builders' Library
entries.why: First-hand accounts of operating large systems, which is the closest thing to production experience available as reading material.

entries.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework
entries.why: A structured checklist across reliability, performance, security, and cost that is useful for auditing a design you have just drawn.

entries.title: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know
entries.why: The canonical order-of-magnitude table. Treat the absolute values as dated but the ratios as still correct, which is what estimation actually relies on.

entries.title: The System Design Primer
entries.why: The breadth reference this curriculum is partly built from, best used for vocabulary coverage rather than as a technical authority.

entries.title: Twitter Snowflake
entries.why: The original implementation the bit layout comes from, including how it handled clock regression — worth reading before reciting the scheme.

entries.title: How Discord Stores Billions of Messages
entries.why: A concrete production account of partitioning message history by channel and time bucket, matching the storage step in the chat dry run.

entries.title: Google Crawlers Overview
entries.why: How a crawler at real scale identifies itself and paces requests, which grounds the politeness and per-host delay logic.

entries.title: Elasticsearch Reference
entries.why: Authoritative on inverted indexes, analyzers, and suggesters, and the practical difference between search and autocomplete workloads.

entries.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd Edition
entries.why: The single best book on data-system trade-offs, and the source most worth reading end to end if you only read one thing on this list.

entries.title: Primer on Latency and Bandwidth (High Performance Browser Networking)
entries.why: Where the time in a web request actually goes — propagation, last-mile latency, and why round trips rather than bandwidth dominate — with measured figures rather than rules of thumb.
